Doctor: Hello, how are you feeling today?
Patient: I'm not feeling well, doctor.
Doctor: I see here that you were admitted to our hospital with a history of worsening cough and phlegm production, is that correct?
Patient: Yes, I've been coughing a lot and producing more phlegm than usual.
Doctor: And you mentioned choking on an iron pill, is that what caused the cough and phlegm production?
Patient: Yes, that's when it started.
Doctor: I also see that you have a history of hypertension, anemia, and immunoglobulin deficiency. Did you have any chest X-rays or CT scans done?
Patient: Yes, I had a chest X-ray done but it was unremarkable. Then I had a CT scan done which showed ground glass infiltrates in the right lower lobe.
Doctor: Ah, I see. Based on the CT scan, you underwent a flexible bronchoscopy. Can you tell me what the results of that were?
Patient: The bronchoscopy showed distal right bronchus intermedius necrosis and stenosis with near-complete obstruction of distal RBI.
Doctor: I also see that there was blackish pigmentation noted in the bronchial mucosa secondary to the iron deposition given your history of aspirating the iron pill. The pathology of the bronchial mucosa was reported as “ulceration and necrosis of bronchial wall, with acute inflammation, fibrinous exudate and prominent stromal iron deposition”. Did you undergo any further procedures?
Patient: Yes, I had a rigid bronchoscopy for cryo-debridement of necrotic tissues with mitomycin application to the lesion. Then I had two follow-up bronchoscopies done four weeks apart which showed worsening fibrosis and stenosis of the RBI. Bronchoscopic balloon dilation was attempted with minimal improvement.
Doctor: I see. Based on the results of your tests and procedures, it seems that you have a serious condition. I will discuss your treatment options with you and your family.

Doctor: I see here that you were first seen in our service in 2012 for a second opinion regarding the treatment of your cardiac arrhythmias. Can you tell me a bit more about your medical history?
Patient: Sure. I have mental retardation, delay of psychomotor development, and a progressive dorso-lumbar scoliosis that was corrected with orthopedic surgery when I was 15 years and 5 months old.

This can cause your heart rate to be slower than usual. Finally, an electrophysiological study was conducted in our institution, showing atrioventricular conduction abnormalities with episodes of Wenckebach atrioventricular block. AH interval was measured at 76 ms and HV interval at 53 ms. There was a duality of the atrioventricular conduction without induction of atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, with or without isoprenaline. Do you understand what that means?
Patient: Not really, no.
Doctor: Essentially, the study showed that your heart has some abnormalities in how it conducts electrical signals. This can cause some of the symptoms you've been experiencing. We'll need to keep monitoring your heart and potentially adjust your treatment plan.

Doctor: Hi, I'm Dr. Hernandez. How are you feeling today?
Patient: Hi, doctor. I'm feeling fine. Just a little nervous.
Doctor: That's understandable. You were referred to me for an evaluation of an asymptomatic retinal hemorrhage detected in your right eye. Can you tell me about your medical history?
Patient: Sure. I don't have any major medical issues. My eyes have been healthy up until now.
Doctor: Okay, that's good to know. I see from your records that you have a history of complete posterior vitreous detachment in your right eye. Is that correct?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: Your best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. That's great news. I'm going to perform an anterior segment examination and applanation tensions to check for any abnormalities. 
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: After the examination, I found that everything was unremarkable. However, during the ophthalmoscopic examination of your right eye, I identified subretinal hemorrhage surrounding a pigment epithelial detachment (PED) located above the superotemporal vascular arcade.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: It means that there is bleeding and fluid accumulation in the area behind your retina. I also performed spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan with angiographic flow overlay to confirm the diagnosis. 
Patient: And what did those tests show?
Doctor: They demonstrated the presence of a PED accompanied by irregularities of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) profile. The OCT B-scan with angiographic flow overlay showed a peaked PED with intrinsic flow signal. 
Patient: I see.
Doctor: I also examined your left eye and found a PED nasal to the optic nerve characterized by a dome-shaped elevation of the RPE with a shallow irregular portion on SD-OCT. The angiographic flow overlay revealed intrinsic flow signal. 
Patient: What about the small drusen?
Doctor: Ah, yes. I did see multiple, small, cuticular drusen appearing as small hypoautofluorescent dots on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) in both eyes along the vascular arcades. 
Patient: What should we do now?
Doctor: Based on the results of the Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA), which showed focal areas of hyperfluorescence within the PEDs, indicative of AT1, and the OCT angiography en face slab, which demonstrated aneurysmal dilatation arising from a type 1 neovascular network, particularly evident in the right eye with active lesions, we need to initiate treatment with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy for your right eye. 
Patient: Okay, what does that involve?
Doctor: It's a type of injection that will be administered directly into the eye to help reduce the bleeding and fluid accumulation. You will need to come back for follow-up appointments to monitor your progress. 
Patient: Alright, I understand. 
Doctor: If you have any questions or concerns, don't hesitate to call our office. 
Patient: Thank you, doctor. 
Doctor: You're welcome. Take care. 
Patient's family: Excuse me, doctor. We're the patient's family. We're sorry to inform you that the patient has passed away due to complications related to the retinal hemorrhage.

Doctor: I understand. We performed an Arterial Doppler and found severe stenosis in your left superficial femoral artery and popliteal artery. We started you on cilostazol, but your symptoms didn't improve. We then did an Arteriography and found there was occlusion of the left popliteal artery.

Doctor: It means that the blood flow in your leg was blocked, which caused your pain. We suspected Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome (PAES) and performed some maneuvers during the study to confirm the diagnosis.

Doctor: We found that dorsiflexion and plantar extension of your ankle caused the cessation of the collateral and distal popliteal artery flow. When we returned the ankle to neutral position, the occlusion ceased and flow was restored. These findings confirmed the diagnosis of PAES with resulting popliteal artery occlusion.
Patient: I see. What was the treatment?
Doctor: We performed a popliteal artery bypass with a reverse great saphenous vein, and your symptoms have now resolved.
Patient: That's great news. What should I do next?
Doctor: We'll need to monitor your condition and make sure that your symptoms don't come back. It's important that you continue to take any prescribed medication and follow a healthy lifestyle.

Patient: I'm not feeling too well, Doctor. I'm feeling fatigued and have been experiencing chest tightness for the past 7 days.
Doctor: I see. Can you tell me more about your symptoms? Have you experienced anything similar before?
Patient: No, I haven't had anything like this before.
Doctor: Okay. I see from your medical history that you don't have any intellectual disability or a history of seizures. Can you tell me what your blood pressure is?
Patient: My blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg.
Doctor: Alright. During your physical examination, we noticed that you had typical facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) and multiple periungual fibromas. We also noticed obvious abdominal distention. Have you experienced any discomfort or pain in these areas?
Patient: Yes, I've been feeling discomfort in my abdomen.
Doctor: I see. Your biochemical laboratory test demonstrated renal insufficiency. Your serum creatinine levels are high, at 3.1 mg/dL, and your estimated glomerular filtration rate is low, at 17.1 ml/min/1.73 m2, estimated by CKD-EPI formula. You also have moderate anemia, with a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL.
Patient: What does that mean, Doctor?
Doctor: It means that your kidneys are not functioning properly and that you have a low red blood cell count. We conducted an Ultrasonography of your kidneys and found a heterogeneous mass with a large echogenic fatty component and a less echogenic soft-tissue component with prominent vessels within it. This is suggestive of giant bilateral renal angiomyolipomas (AML).
Patient: What is that?
Doctor: It means that you have large masses in both of your kidneys. We also found highly vascular fatty masses on Color Doppler scans. Additionally, Ultrasonography of your left eye showed a hyperechogenic lesion with posterior shadowing due to calcifications. We also found a hamartoma with central calcifications and a surrounding translucent zone in your left eye, suggesting the retinal hamartoma.
Patient: That sounds serious, Doctor.
Doctor: Yes, it is. We conducted a non-contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of your abdomen and confirmed the Ultrasonography diagnosis of giant bilateral renal AMLs with prominent fatty components and internal prominent vessels. We also found multiple variable-sized air-filled cysts throughout the parenchyma in both of your lungs, which is consistent with lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) on lung CT.
Patient: What does that mean for me, Doctor?
Doctor: Unfortunately, your conditions are quite serious and require immediate attention. We will need to monitor your kidney function closely and potentially perform surgery to remove the masses. We will also need to monitor your lung function and potentially treat your LAM. We will keep you and your family informed throughout the process.
Patient: Okay, thank you, Doctor.

In addition, upon probing the pancreatic duct in the tail of the pancreas, the probe did not slide smoothly, suggestive of additional growths in the duct. Doctor: Good afternoon, how can I help you today?
Patient: Hi, doctor. I've been having symptoms of right ear congestion, pulsatile tinnitus, and mild hearing loss.
Doctor: Okay, let me perform a neurological examination. Ah, I see that you have weakness of cranial nerves X and XII. We need to do some imaging to investigate this further.
Patient: Okay, doctor.
Doctor: We performed a Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and identified a 4.2 x 4.7 x 4.1 cm lobulated mass centered at the cerebellopontine angle that was hypointense on T1-weighted, heterogeneous on T2-weighted, and avidly enhancing on post-contrast images.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: It means that we need to do an Octreoscan to confirm whether this is a paraganglioma or not.
Patient: What's an Octreoscan?
Doctor: It's a test that shows increased tracer uptake in the mass centered in the region of the right jugular foramen, which supports the suspected diagnosis of paraganglioma.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: We also did a Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) and found that there was a surprising lack of vascularity associated with the tumor. However, we did find an incidental discovery of a Cognard IIa+b dural arteriovenous fistula in the right posterior fossa associated with an occluded right sigmoid sinus.
Patient: What does that mean for me?
Doctor: It means that due to the extensive volume of tumor, you will need to undergo a staged surgical resection.
Patient: Okay, doctor.
Doctor: The first surgery will include a modified radical right neck dissection, right superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection, as well as the initial approach to the tumor and partial extradural resection. One week later, you will undergo the second stage surgery where the tumor will be radically resected using a right transcochlear approach. The right sigmoid sinus will be ligated. The facial nerve will be mobilized and transposed.
Patient: Is there anything else I should know?
Doctor: Yes, after the surgery, we will do a Postoperative MRI to confirm complete resection of the tumor. Histological analysis of samples from both surgeries will be done to confirm the tumor not to be a paraganglioma, but instead a schwannoma.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
Doctor: She had a long recovery from the surgery due to the lower cranial nerve palsies but has shown gradual improvement. Her latest follow-up MRI (48 months from surgery) showed no evidence of recurrent tumor; however, there was some residual posterior fossa DA.
